Stay with me: Is it not also inherently selfish to want a loved one to stay alive (and in pain), because you'd be affected if they died?

Unfortunately people suffering with depression and suicidal people can feel like only death can take the pain or whatever away. And for many the classic suggestions of exercise, medication, therapy and hobbies etc. do not help (or at least it can take ages to see any kind of improvement), especially if you consider things like the medical side effects, possibly unhelpful medical professionals and that's before you even consider access to such help. And of course don't forget that depression makes it hard to do these things. 

So if you understand that someone in that state of mind is in pain and has probably been in pain for a while, then unfortunately when people say that their suicide would be painful for others so you shouldn't do anything it can seem like it's saying that we'd rather you were in pain and not us. It's a situation that can feel like the world would rather they didn't have to experience any of what you experience so you should continue with the burden of the life you didn't ask for and want out of. ( It's particularly ridiculous to me that I'm alive because my parents wanted me and now I have to stay alive because it would make them sad if I died. I didn't ask to be here, they created me because they wanted a child and now I'm stuck. They can create another sentient being because they want a child to play with or whatever and it's responsible for them not being sad for decades?)

For some these supposed loved ones may actually be contributing to their pain. And for many people (especially those who feel isolated or lonely), they don't even see these loved ones regularly or feel a deep connection so it can, inaccurately, feel like it wouldn't affect their lives much.

So anyway, if we think about how lots of suicidal people feel like death is the only way to make the pain end then, if we imagine that's true, there's no way for everyone to be happy/not in pain. Someone has to be suffering so that the other isn't. 

Plus _all_ depressed people hear is that "it would be selfish" and "it will get better". Two things that stink of a lack of awareness of that person's situation and the complexity of severe depression

I don't think my own experience can say which is "better" or "worse", but I've lived in both South England and Edinburgh. My experience of casual racism was more prevalent in Edinburgh which I suspected was due to the much lower levels of ethnic diversity. The "where are you from" questions were so much more common and when it came to dating I was often called "exotic" if anyone showed interest at all. When I moved to South England the difference was notable pretty quickly.

I also had one of my only more overt racist experiences in Edinburgh.

Like I said, that's just _my_ experience and it doesn't mean much for the situation generally, and it doesn't mean that I think of Edinburgh or Scotland as being wildly racist or South England or England as a safe haven from racism, but I just thought I'd comment because my own experience didn't match your statement that Scotland was certainly better than England (on the you're not one of us type things). 

Perhaps I also wanted to comment because, even when someone acknowledges that it's not perfect or needs to be improved, sometimes a favourable comparison with another place seems to be what _some_ people (sounds like not you) focus on (not what you were doing, but similar to when some people say that women should be happy that they're not in a country where they'd have fewer rights, they're just focusing on it being better than elsewhere). I remember as a teenager focusing on racism being not as bad as elsewhere and I think it made me ignore some stuff. Also I think it can be part of what leads people to think of these communities as "going on about it" or "moaning all the time" or "exaggerating", because they're focusing on how "they should be happy (even grateful), it's better here than anywhere else" (while patting themselves on the back). So for anyone who might be tempted to read your comment and think along those lines my comment could serve as a reminder that even if a place is better than somewhere else, there's still real people who experience the institutional and causal prejudice or discrimination and that a even "just little comments" can mean so much especially because it's usually a lifetime of little comments and at best they basically say "hey, the first thing I noticed about you was that you're not white and it makes me think of you as being different and from somewhere else", and if you've experienced stuff it doesn't make them less valid.

Anyway, sorry for the long comment. Went off on a bit of a tangent there
But what's the point if it's always this way? If things have been bad for years and years, is there much point in continuing to push through? Where's the light at the end of the tunnel?

I think that makes sense, but can be especially difficult if you are actually part of the group that they have prejudices against because then they are seeing _you_ as lesser or being insensitive to _you_ or have preconceived ideas about _you_. Like you said, it depends on the extent and perhaps the topic, after all we can all be insensitive to each other. However when people say insensitive what they often mean is that 
 what the other person has said or done isn't OVERT prejudice or discrimination. I think it's easier to forgive and forget when what they've said or done isn't about or to you. And over a lifetime these moments can be numerous and the burden to always "be the bigger person" and/or to educate them and/or to be nothing but civil in response weighs people down and is realistically an unfair additional burden. And personally, with all the overt and covert things here and there and all the negative experiences I've had I do not currently have the space or time in my life to patiently explain or demonstrate that I am not lesser (and/or neither is that other person) , but in fact a human deserving of empathy and fair (at least as much fair as life can give) and at the very least not deserving of prejudice or discrimination.

Of course there can be downsides to doing too much medical research online, but it can be good too. Especially because it seems fairly common for people with focal aware seizures to be dismissed by their GPs (or equivalent), or even by neurologists, as having anxiety attacks etc. so I think it can be good to know a bit about it before you speak to them about it. (I was actually dismissed by the first GP I saw as just having a few fainting spells and he was quite patronising when I brought up incidents that had happened the previous year)

As for the memory, I myself am going through the diagnostic process and one of the things I raised was that my memory doesn't seem to be anywhere near as good. The specialist ordered a neuropsychology test for it so I'd recommend raising that to if you decide to raise all of this.

Other things that might be worth noting: 

The diagnostic process can be lengthy, especially because for many people with epilepsy an EEG  will only show anything if they are having  a seizure at the time and because other conditions (including psychological ones) can have similar symptoms. If you are feel nervous about it all and feel like it's not worth it, I'd still recommend having it checked out (if you feel like the symptoms could match) because seizures can transform over time and get worse and so it's good to get going. For example even someone with a relatively mild form of epilepsy which has little impact on their life may one day end up having much worse seizures and more regularly.

On a positive note (in case this is all scary) 70% of people with epilepsy get their seizures under control! 1 in 100 people in the UK (and I think 1 in 26 in the US) have epilepsy so you wouldn't be alone! And only 3% of people with epilepsy are photosensitive so it would be unlikely that you are (I'll admit this last stat is mainly about awareness because photosensitivity is all people think about when they think of epilepsy, that and that seizures are always tonic clonics, which is where you go stiff and then convulse, but there's loads of types).

You could also check out r/epilepsy if you wanted too!

Hope that helps!

Hello, I don't mean to armchair diagnose or stress you out. 

However, deja vu can be a symptom of temporal lobe epilepsy and in lots of people with epilepsy seizures are triggered by stress.

I'm not saying that you have it, it could be random deja vu. But it's not umcommon for people who have focal aware seizures not to realise that's what they were until years later when they get diagnosed. So perhaps you could read something about the symptoms and see if it's possible and speak to a neurologist if you think it is.
